items.title: Machine speed attacks require machine speed detection and response
items.description: Attackers can steal credentials and begin exfiltrating data within minutes, often before security teams can respond. Exaforce examines real-world attacks involving stolen GitHub tokens, malicious AI installers, and MFA phishing, explaining why faster detection and automated containment are critical. [...]

items.title: North Korean Hackers Use Post-Quantum Encryption to Hide New Malware From Security Tools
items.description: North Korean-linked Lazarus hackers are using post-quantum cryptography in a malware delivery chain designed to conceal later-stage payloads from security tools. The technique appeared in Operation FlashHole, a campaign targeting organizations in South Korea. Instead of relying on encryption alone to hide files on disk, the malware uses a modern key-establishment method to protect payloads […]…

items.title: A Hacker Tried to Turn an AI Chatbot Into a Tool for Attacking Other Servers
items.description: An exposed artificial intelligence platform can give an intruder more than a place to send messages. If it connects to stored credentials, company data, or network tools, the platform may also provide a route toward those resources. A recent honeypot investigation shows how an attacker tried to use an AI agent to study real infrastructure […] The post A Hacker Tried to Turn an AI Chatbot Into a…

items.title: The AI Agent Nobody Owns: Watch Expert Webinar On Your Newest Insider Threat
items.description: Right now, there is probably an AI agent running on a laptop somewhere in your network. It stores API keys and database passwords, can access your internal systems, and works without anyone watching. Nobody reviewed its access. Nobody owns it. If an employee had that much reach with that little oversight, you would call it an insider risk. So why do we still call the agent a productivity tool?

The replacement keeps the bank app’s name and version, but contains extra code designed to interfere with security checks. OpenCode connects to MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers to add outside tools, and such code would run with the developer's own access. items.title: LiteLLM Suspects GitHub Token Leak in AI Gateway Logs Behind Malicious Package Release
items.description: LiteLLM on Wednesday disclosed that threat actors compromised "multiple independent security controls" to push a malicious version of the Python package containing a credential stealer and a backdoor. On October 21, 2026, LiteLLM's release pipeline was compromised to push 1.107.0 to the Docker Hub registry and the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. The incident took place around 4:00 a.m.
